strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a practical clinical NLP bottleneck: limited access to annotated health records. Its 8,767 synthetic snippets, 15 annotation categories, and accompanying spans, presence labels, temporal attributes, and rationales constitute a useful resource contribution.

The central augmentation claim has credible support on real clinical datasets across several model architectures. For example, prompt-based RoBERTa improves from 56.17 to 91.20 macro-F on MIMIC-SBDH, while T5 improves from 65.34 to 67.40 exact-match macro-F on VA-SBDH. Reporting three-run means and standard deviations strengthens this evidence.

Expert review of all 1,755 synthetic test examples is substantial. Correcting erroneous annotations, adding missing mentions, reviewing rationales, and publishing category-specific error analyses provide useful information about the resource’s limitations.

The specified GPT-4 snapshot, 45 seed examples, generation prompt, filtering threshold, dataset mappings, training configurations, and repository link provide substantial reproducibility support. The resource and demonstrated augmentation benefits support a Findings recommendation.
weaknesses: The headline improvements need qualification. The 62.36% gain is relative, corresponding to 35.03 macro-F points from a weak baseline; the strongest baseline already reaches 90.49 macro-F. Much of the rare-category improvement comes from housing insecurity, with only 18 positive test examples. Conversely, the strongest NER encoder improves only from 70.21 to 70.43 exact-match macro-F. Test-sample uncertainty and paired significance analyses would help distinguish robust improvements from small fluctuations.

The experiments do not establish the advantage over straightforward alternatives such as class reweighting, oversampling, or longer baseline training. MLC models receive 40 additional synthetic-data epochs before eight target-data epochs. These comparisons demonstrate augmentation utility, but the compute-efficiency claim requires accounting for this additional training and data-generation cost.

The human evaluation needs clearer interpretation and adjudication details. The 71.06% human alignment uses a denominator that includes newly added annotations, whereas GPT-4’s 90.78% self-agreement excludes missing annotations; these percentages are not directly comparable. The reported 77.80% inter-annotator agreement lacks a clear disagreement-resolution procedure, and Appendix D.1 permits retaining different plausible categories depending on GPT-4’s original choice. This limits confidence in treating the reviewed set as a consistent gold-standard benchmark.

Several advertised capabilities remain weakly validated. The experiments retain only presence=yes annotations and do not evaluate temporal prediction, leaving negation and temporality largely untested. DSS yields only 0.66 and 0.58 macro-F-point improvements on synthetic test data. These results offer limited evidence for the stronger claim of transferring reasoning capability; evaluating extraction predictions on real clinical text would not require reference rationales.

Reproducibility and reporting need tightening. Exact prompt-based fine-tuning templates/verbalizers and DSS loss weighting are not specified in the manuscript, while private VA-SBDH restricts independent replication of the NER results. The reported split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767 examples. Such discrepancies should be reconciled with the released data.

The privacy motivation requires a consistent account of seed provenance. Appendix A.3 describes expert-written examples, the generation prompt describes examples collected from clinical notes, and Section 7.3 says they were based on VHA EHR notes. Clarifying whether these were newly composed, paraphrased, or extracted is necessary to substantiate the claim of eliminating real-world EHR data from generation.
